method: OPEN AND QUOTED from Cheng K, Rosenthal P (University of California San Francisco), Hepatology Communications 7(12):e0314 'Diagnosis and management of Alagille and progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis' (published 7 December 2023). Every pass claim is machine re-checkable. LICENCE: CC BY 4.0 (read at Europe PMC fullTextXML <license> element for PMC10984671).

claims.claim: PFIC is a group of single-gene disorders of canalicular bile acid transport or secretion; the intermittent form is BRIC and the chronic form is PFIC.
claims.source_text: PFIC refers to a heterogenous group of monogenic disorders that result from defects in canalicular bile acid trafficking and/or secretion. Any interruption or disruption in the process can result in intermittent cholestatic jaundice such as benign recurrent intrahepatic cholestasis (BRIC), or chronic liver disease (PFIC).
claims.locator: Cheng K, Rosenthal P (University of California San Francisco), Hepatology Communications 7(12):e0314, 'Diagnosis and management of Alagille and progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis', published 7 December 2023, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10984671/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: PFIC disorders are autosomal recessive. Pruritus is the most significant clinical feature and can affect school, sleep and quality of life.
claims.source_text: PFIC disorders are autosomal recessive … Pruritus remains the most significant clinical manifestation of these disorders and can affect school, sleep, and overall quality of life.
claims.locator: Cheng K, Rosenthal P (University of California San Francisco), Hepatology Communications 7(12):e0314, 'Diagnosis and management of Alagille and progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis', published 7 December 2023, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10984671/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Serum GGT separates the types:** PFIC1 and PFIC2 have low or normal GGT; PFIC3 (ABCB4/MDR3) is distinguished by raised GGT.
claims.source_text: Serum gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT) is typically normal with minimally elevated serum aminotransferases. … Like those with PFIC1, patients with PFIC2 also have low serum GGT, and normal or near-normal serum cholesterol levels. … It is distinguished from PFIC1 and PFIC2 by elevation in serum GGT.
claims.locator: Cheng K, Rosenthal P (University of California San Francisco), Hepatology Communications 7(12):e0314, 'Diagnosis and management of Alagille and progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis', published 7 December 2023, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10984671/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **PFIC1 (ATP8B1)** starts in infancy and typically progresses to cirrhosis by the second decade, with extrahepatic features (pancreatitis, diarrhoea, sensorineural hearing loss) that can persist or worsen after liver transplant.
claims.source_text: Patients with PFIC1 typically present with cholestasis that starts in infancy and progresses to cirrhosis, typically by the second decade of life. … which leads to patients having extrahepatic manifestations such as recurrent pancreatitis, diarrhea, and sensorineural hearing loss. These extrahepatic manifestations often persist and can even worsen after a liver transplant.
claims.locator: Cheng K, Rosenthal P (University of California San Francisco), Hepatology Communications 7(12):e0314, 'Diagnosis and management of Alagille and progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis', published 7 December 2023, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10984671/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **PFIC2 (ABCB11/BSEP)** is the most common form, usually presenting in the neonatal period; without treatment it progresses rapidly to cirrhosis.
claims.source_text: This is the most common form of PFIC and typically presents in the neonatal period with progressive cholestasis. … Without treatment, these patients have rapid progression to cirrhosis.
claims.locator: Cheng K, Rosenthal P (University of California San Francisco), Hepatology Communications 7(12):e0314, 'Diagnosis and management of Alagille and progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis', published 7 December 2023, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10984671/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Fat-soluble vitamin malabsorption can cause catastrophic bleeding (vitamin K), rickets (vitamin D) and neuromuscular dysfunction (vitamin E).**
claims.source_text: Fat-soluble vitamin malabsorption can lead to catastrophic bleeding (vitamin K deficiency), rickets (vitamin D deficiency), and neuromuscular dysfunction (vitamin E deficiency).
claims.locator: Cheng K, Rosenthal P (University of California San Francisco), Hepatology Communications 7(12):e0314, 'Diagnosis and management of Alagille and progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis', published 7 December 2023, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10984671/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: Failure to thrive and malnutrition are common and need close monitoring and supplementation, especially with **formula containing medium-chain triglycerides**, plus fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E and K). Some children need nasogastric or gastrostomy feeds.
claims.source_text: Failure to thrive and malnutrition are common for children with Alagille syndrome and PFIC and require close monitoring and supplementation, especially with formula containing medium-chain triglycerides. Many also require vitamin supplements, especially fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, and K). Some patients may require nasogastric feeds or gastrostomy tube feedings to reach caloric intake goals.
claims.locator: Cheng K, Rosenthal P (University of California San Francisco), Hepatology Communications 7(12):e0314, 'Diagnosis and management of Alagille and progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis', published 7 December 2023, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10984671/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: Skin emollients, trimmed fingernails and avoiding hot baths help minimise itching and excoriation.
claims.source_text: Skin emollients, trimmed fingernails, and avoiding hot baths can help minimize itching and excoriation.
claims.locator: Cheng K, Rosenthal P (University of California San Francisco), Hepatology Communications 7(12):e0314, 'Diagnosis and management of Alagille and progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis', published 7 December 2023, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10984671/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: Antihistamine and ursodeoxycholic acid can be trialled but are typically not very effective alone in PFIC. **Ursodeoxycholic acid 10–20 mg/kg daily** may improve liver biochemistry but helps little in severe pruritus with PFIC1 or PFIC2; in PFIC3 it has normalised liver tests in half of patients.
claims.source_text: Similarly, antihistamine and ursodeoxycholic acid can be trialed but are typically not very efficacious alone for children with PFIC. Ursodeoxycholic acid at daily dosage of 10-20 mg/kg may improve liver biochemical markers, but has little benefit in those with severe pruritus and PFIC1 or PFIC2. In those with PFIC3, ursodeoxycholic acid has been noted to lead to normalization of liver tests in half of the patients.
claims.locator: Cheng K, Rosenthal P (University of California San Francisco), Hepatology Communications 7(12):e0314, 'Diagnosis and management of Alagille and progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis', published 7 December 2023, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10984671/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: Other medicines to consider include rifampicin, cholestyramine or antihistamines. Cholestyramine must be given at least 2 hours apart from other medicines and increases the risk of fat-soluble vitamin deficiency.
claims.source_text: Like patients with Alagille syndrome, other medications to consider include rifampin, cholestyramine, or antihistamines. … Bile acid-binding resins such as cholestyramine may be helpful, but this can affect other medication absorption and must be given separately for at least 2 hours. It also increases the risk of fat-soluble vitamin deficiencies and needs to be monitored closely.
claims.locator: Cheng K, Rosenthal P (University of California San Francisco), Hepatology Communications 7(12):e0314, 'Diagnosis and management of Alagille and progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis', published 7 December 2023, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10984671/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: Ileal bile acid transporter inhibitors have shown efficacy for refractory pruritus in PFIC; two are available, maralixibat and odevixibat.
claims.source_text: recent medical advancements in the use of ileal bile acid transport inhibitors have shown efficacy for the treatment of refractory pruritus in Alagille syndrome and PFIC. … There are 2 medications currently available, maralixibat and odevixibat.
claims.locator: Cheng K, Rosenthal P (University of California San Francisco), Hepatology Communications 7(12):e0314, 'Diagnosis and management of Alagille and progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis', published 7 December 2023, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10984671/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: Odevixibat is approved (in the source's jurisdiction) for pruritus in all types of PFIC from 3 months of age.
claims.source_text: It is currently approved for pruritus in children with Alagille syndrome (12 mo and older) and all types of PFIC (3 mo and older).
claims.locator: Cheng K, Rosenthal P (University of California San Francisco), Hepatology Communications 7(12):e0314, 'Diagnosis and management of Alagille and progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis', published 7 December 2023, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10984671/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: In the phase 3 PEDFIC trial (PFIC1 or PFIC2), odevixibat improved pruritus by week 4, with sustained improvement, lower aminotransferases and better growth and sleep; no serious adverse events were reported.
claims.source_text: In the phase 3, randomized, double-blind PEDFIC study, children with PFIC1 or PFIC2 were assigned to either placebo, odevixibat 40 μg/kg, or odevixibat 120 μg/kg over 24-week period. Treatment with odevixibat led to improvement in pruritus observed by week 4, and sustained improvement. … Those who received odevixibat also had reduction in serum aminotransferase levels, as well as improved growth and sleep parameters. There were no serious adverse events reported
claims.locator: Cheng K, Rosenthal P (University of California San Francisco), Hepatology Communications 7(12):e0314, 'Diagnosis and management of Alagille and progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis', published 7 December 2023, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10984671/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Odevixibat dosing: start at 40 µg/kg once daily; if pruritus has not improved after 3 months, increase in 40 µg/kg steps up to 120 µg/kg once daily.**
claims.source_text: The recommended starting dose for odevixibat is 40 µg/kg. If no improvement in pruritis is noted after 3 months, the dosage can be increased in 40 µg/kg increments up to 120 µg/kg once daily.
claims.locator: Cheng K, Rosenthal P (University of California San Francisco), Hepatology Communications 7(12):e0314, 'Diagnosis and management of Alagille and progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis', published 7 December 2023, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10984671/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: Maralixibat in PFIC1 and PFIC2 (INDIGO) gave a response that varied by subtype; BSEP deficiency with residual function did best.
claims.source_text: This study found a variable response depending on PFIC subtype, as well as BSEP mutation. Those with BSEP deficiency, especially those with residual BSEP function, experienced significant and sustained improvement in pruritis, biochemical laboratory parameters, growth, and quality of life.
claims.locator: Cheng K, Rosenthal P (University of California San Francisco), Hepatology Communications 7(12):e0314, 'Diagnosis and management of Alagille and progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis', published 7 December 2023, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10984671/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **PFIC2 carries a risk of hepatocellular carcinoma and cholangiocarcinoma, as early as 10 months of age**: screen with tumour markers (including alpha-fetoprotein) and imaging.
claims.source_text: patients with PFIC2 are at risk of developing HCC and cholangiocarcinoma and this can occur as early as 10 months of age … Due to the risk of HCC in those with PFIC2, it is important to consider screening for hepatic malignancy with tumor markers (including alpha-fetoprotein) and imaging.
claims.locator: Cheng K, Rosenthal P (University of California San Francisco), Hepatology Communications 7(12):e0314, 'Diagnosis and management of Alagille and progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis', published 7 December 2023, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10984671/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: For pruritus refractory to medicines, surgical biliary diversion can be considered. After partial external biliary diversion one study reported improved pruritus in 81% with PFIC1 and 76% with PFIC2; no non-transplant operation has been shown superior to another.
claims.source_text: For children and adults with Alagille syndrome or PFIC who have pruritus refractory to medical management, surgical intervention can be considered to aim to disrupt the enterohepatic circulation of bile acids to prevent intestinal re-uptake of bile acids and therefore decrease total body bile acids and allow pruritus to improve. … one study reporting 81% of those with PFIC1 and 76% of those with PFIC2 having transient or sustained improvement of pruritus. … there is no evidence of superiority for one type of nontransplant surgical intervention compared to another.
claims.locator: Cheng K, Rosenthal P (University of California San Francisco), Hepatology Communications 7(12):e0314, 'Diagnosis and management of Alagille and progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis', published 7 December 2023, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10984671/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Hepatoportoenterostomy (Kasai) is not indicated in PFIC** and can increase liver injury.
claims.source_text: Hepatoportoenterostomy, a surgical operation commonly done for biliary atresia, is not indicated in Alagille syndrome or PFIC and can increase the amount of liver injury.
claims.locator: Cheng K, Rosenthal P (University of California San Francisco), Hepatology Communications 7(12):e0314, 'Diagnosis and management of Alagille and progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis', published 7 December 2023, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10984671/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: Liver transplant is considered for end-stage liver disease, HCC or refractory pruritus. With severe FIC1 or BSEP deficiency only 50% survive with their native liver at 10 years.
claims.source_text: Liver transplant is typically considered when patients with PFIC have end-stage liver disease, HCC, or refractory pruritus. For those with severe FIC1 and BSEP deficiency, native liver survival beyond childhood is unlikely with only 50% of patients surviving with a native liver at the 10-year mark.
claims.locator: Cheng K, Rosenthal P (University of California San Francisco), Hepatology Communications 7(12):e0314, 'Diagnosis and management of Alagille and progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis', published 7 December 2023, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10984671/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **In PFIC1 without cirrhosis, strongly consider non-transplant surgery first**, because transplant can bring pancreatitis, allograft steatosis and diarrhoea. In PFIC2, anti-BSEP antibodies can cause recurrent disease after transplant.
claims.source_text: However, for those with FIC1 disease, liver transplant can lead to further complications such as pancreatitis, allograft steatosis, and diarrhea related to extrahepatic expression of ATP8B1. In those with PFIC1 without cirrhosis, nontransplant surgical options should be strongly considered before a liver transplant. … anti-BSEP antibodies can develop and lead to recurrent liver disease after liver transplant.
claims.locator: Cheng K, Rosenthal P (University of California San Francisco), Hepatology Communications 7(12):e0314, 'Diagnosis and management of Alagille and progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis', published 7 December 2023, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10984671/, retrieved 2026-09-23
